title: Mind the Gap: Mixtures of Gaussians in Approximate Differential Privacy
claim: Standard additive noise distributions are smooth and broad; our designed mixtures concentrate mass near zero while still satisfying the same privacy guarantee.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, shared x-axis, legends beneath each panel
description: Three side-by-side line plots share the same x-axis from -3 to 3, and each shows a noise probability density with a shaded fill. The left panel shows baselines: a wide, flat blue Gaussian and a taller green analytic Gaussian, both smooth bell curves. The middle panel shows a dark red, blocky step-function density from numerical optimization, peaked at zero with stepped shoulders. The right panel shows the proposed distributions: a red multi-Gaussian mixture with a sharp central spike and smaller side bumps at ±1 and ±2, and a gray quasi-Gaussian with a flat, two-humped top. Legends sit below each panel. The eye goes first to the tall red spike on the right.
caption: Different noise distributions that guarantee (1, 0.1)-DP for a query with ∆= 1.
abstract: We design a class of additive noise mechanisms that satisfy \((\varepsilon, Î´)\)-differential privacy (DP) for scalar, real-valued query functions with known sensitivities, with a particular focus on moderate and low-privacy regimes. These mechanisms, which we call \textit{mixture mechanisms}, are constructed by mixing multiple Gaussian distributions that share the same variance but differ in their means and mixture weights. The resulting distributions can be interpreted as convex combinations of a zero-mean Gaussian (as used in the analytic Gaussian mechanism) and additional Gaussians whose means depend on the sensitivity of the query function. We derive tight conditions on the variances required for \((\varepsilon, Î´)\)-DP and provide efficient algorithms to compute them. Compared to the analytic Gaussian mechanism, our mechanisms yield substantially lower expected noise amplitudes (\(l_1\)-loss) and variances (\(l_2\)-loss for zero-mean distributions). In the low-privacy regime that motivates our design, our mechanisms approach optimality, mitigating nearly all of the optimality gap of the analytic Gaussian mechanism.
